1.pericope_label: Then Samuel took a vial of oil, and poured it upon his head, and kissed him, and said, Is it not because the Lord hath anointed thee to be captain over his inheritance? When thou art departed from me to day, then thou shalt find two men by Rachel’s sepulchre in the border of Benjamin at Zelzah; and they will say unto thee, The asses which thou wentest to seek are found: and, lo, thy father hath left the care of the asses, and sorroweth for you, saying, What shall I do for my son? Then shalt thou go on forward from thence, and thou shalt come to the plain of Tabor, and there shall meet thee three men going up to God to Beth–el, one carrying three kids, and another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a bottle of wine: And they will salute thee, and give thee two loaves of bread; which thou shalt receive of their hands.

schools.summary: Ellicott insists the oil was the sacred anointing oil and not common oil, reads the kiss as reverential homage rather than affection, and explains why only founders of dynasties and irregular claimants are recorded as anointed; Delitzsch rejects the conjecture that the terebinth of Tabor is the tree of Deborah.
Gill reports the Jewish view that the tabernacle oil was reserved for the house of David, and that a vial rather than a horn foretold a short reign.

Clarke notes that Saul is styled only a captain and not a king, and explains the salutation from Eastern custom; Wesley reads the kiss as a testimony of sincere affection and "his inheritance" as a reminder that the people were God's and not Saul's.
Henry takes the oil for common oil and makes the vial itself a portent of a brittle and short-lived kingdom, and turns the sepulchre and the two loaves into lessons on mortality and humility.

debates: Whether the oil was the sacred anointing oil of the tabernacle, as Ellicott holds, or common oil, as Gill and Henry take it.
Whether the kiss was affection, as Wesley says, or formal homage, which Ellicott argues on the ground that the two had only just met.
Whether the terebinth of Tabor is the burial tree of Rachel's nurse, a conjecture Ellicott passes on and Delitzsch dismisses as baseless.
outliers: Clarke and Ellicott both note that the Greek treated the place-name Zelzah as a verb and rendered it dancing or springing vehemently.
themes: Then Samuel took a vial of oil, and poured it upon his head, and kissed him, and said, Is it not because the Lord hath anointed thee to be captain over his inheritance?

When thou art departed from me to day, then thou shalt find two men by Rachel’s sepulchre in the border of Benjamin at Zelzah; and they will say unto thee, The asses which thou wentest to seek are found: and, lo, thy father hath left the care of the asses, and sorroweth for you, saying, What shall I do for my son?

Then shalt thou go on forward from thence, and thou shalt come to the plain of Tabor, and there shall meet thee three men going up to God to Beth–el, one carrying three kids, and another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a bottle of wine:
And they will salute thee, and give thee two loaves of bread; which thou shalt receive of their hands.

5.pericope_label: After that thou shalt come to the hill of God, where is the garrison of the Philistines: and it shall come to pass, when thou art come thither to the city, that thou shalt meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp, before them; and they shall prophesy: And the Spirit of the Lord will come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them, and shalt be turned into another man. And let it be, when these signs are come unto thee, that thou do as occasion serve thee; for God is with thee. And thou shalt go down before me to Gilgal; and, behold, I will come down unto thee, to offer burnt offerings, and to sacrifice sacrifices of peace offerings: seven days shalt thou tarry, till I come to thee, and shew thee what thou shalt do.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Delitzsch read "the hill of God" as a proper name, the Gibeah of Saul's own town; Ellicott denies that the young men of the prophetic schools were inspired in the usual sense, holding the schools to have been founded for the higher education of Israel, and refuses to explain the ecstasy by their music, while Delitzsch rejects the contagion explanation as insufficient and calls the change a transformation resembling regeneration.
Gill argues for Geba rather than the Targum's hill of the ark, and also reads the seven days at Gilgal as a permanent rule rather than a single appointment.

Clarke redefines the word prophet from Genesis 20:7 as a man of prayer and teaching rather than of prediction, and says that inattention to this sense has puzzled every commentator he has met; Wesley makes the change a sudden natural endowment of courage and wisdom, and takes the Gilgal command for a standing rule.
Henry questions whether Saul, though made another man, was made a new one.

debates: Where the hill of God was: the hill of the ark, Geba, a height near Gibeah, or Gibeah itself.
What Saul's prophesying was, and whether the word here means prediction at all.
What the seven days at Gilgal refer to: the sacrifice after the Ammonite victory, the later trial of faith, a standing rule for all emergencies, or a conditional instruction.
outliers: Delitzsch reports the observation that ecstatic states are infectious and spread involuntarily, as in the American revivals and the preaching mania in Sweden, only to deny that psychical infection explains this case.
themes: After that thou shalt come to the hill of God, where is the garrison of the Philistines: and it shall come to pass, when thou art come thither to the city, that thou shalt meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp, before them; and they shall prophesy:
And the Spirit of the Lord will come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them, and shalt be turned into another man.

9.pericope_label: And it was so, that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart: and all those signs came to pass that day. And when they came thither to the hill, behold, a company of prophets met him; and the Spirit of God came upon him, and he prophesied among them. And it came to pass, when all that knew him beforetime saw that, behold, he prophesied among the prophets, then the people said one to another, What is this that is come unto the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets? And one of the same place answered and said, But who is their father? Therefore it became a proverb, Is Saul also among the prophets? And when he had made an end of prophesying, he came to the high place. And Saul’s uncle said unto him and to his servant, Whither went ye? And he said, To seek the asses: and when we saw that they were no where, we came to Samuel. And Saul’s uncle said, Tell me, I pray thee, what Samuel said unto you. And Saul said unto his uncle, He told us plainly that the asses were found. But of the matter of the kingdom, whereof Samuel spake, he told him not.

schools.summary: Delitzsch construes "who is their father?" as asking whether the prophets held their gift by birth, rules out the rendering "who is their instructor" as gratuitous, rejects the versions' alteration to "his father", and attributes Saul's silence to unambitious humility rather than fear; Ellicott times the new heart in the morning against the Spirit in the evening and derives the proverb from the later recurrence of the scene.
Gill cites Procopius Gazaeus that the gift of prophecy did not continue with Saul but was given to make him respectable before his election.

Clarke accepts the Greek addition naming Kish, judging that it completes the sense; Wesley explains why only the third sign is narrated, and has Saul return to the high place in the prophets' company.

Henry describes the new heart as the exchange of a husbandman's mind for a statesman's, offers the very reading Delitzsch dismisses, and draws the double moral that the worst are not to be despaired of while a sudden change is not to be relied on.

debates: What "who is their father?" asks, and whether the text should read "their father" or, with the versions, "his father".
Where the proverb came from: this occasion, as Henry holds, or the later repetition of the scene, as Ellicott prefers.
Whether Saul went up to the high place alone for private communing or returned there with the prophets.
outliers: Henry and Ellicott independently hear behind "Is Saul also among the prophets?" the astonishment of those who later found Saul of Tarsus preaching the gospel he had persecuted.
themes: And it was so, that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart: and all those signs came to pass that day.
And when they came thither to the hill, behold, a company of prophets met him; and the Spirit of God came upon him, and he prophesied among them.

17.pericope_label: And Samuel called the people together unto the Lord to Mizpeh; And said unto the children of Israel, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of all kingdoms, and of them that oppressed you: And ye have this day rejected your God, who himself saved you out of all your adversities and your tribulations; and ye have said unto him, Nay, but set a king over us. Now therefore present yourselves before the Lord by your tribes, and by your thousands. And when Samuel had caused all the tribes of Israel to come near, the tribe of Benjamin was taken. When he had caused the tribe of Benjamin to come near by their families, the family of Matri was taken, and Saul the son of Kish was taken: and when they sought him, he could not be found. Therefore they enquired of the Lord further, if the man should yet come thither. And the Lord answered, Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff. And they ran and fetched him thence: and when he stood among the people, he was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward. And Samuel said to all the people, See ye him whom the Lord hath chosen, that there is none like him among all the people? And all the people shouted, and said, God save the king.

schools.summary: Ellicott concedes that a mortal king was needful for the development of Israel's power while insisting the change would never have been necessary but for the nation's apostasy, notes that the method of casting lots is not stated, and sets Saul's stature beside Agamemnon and the later tradition that knows him only as the tall one; Delitzsch explains the choice of Mizpeh from the victory won there by prayer.
Gill takes the assembly for the heads and elders rather than every individual, and reports the conjecture that the Urim and the ark were both present.

Clarke sets out the four stages of the lot and ascribes Saul's hiding to modesty or fear; Wesley reads the choice of an obscure tribe as a mark of divine anger, the kingdom having been forced from God rather than freely given as it was to Judah.
Henry explains why lots were cast although Samuel had already anointed the man, reads the choice of Benjamin against Jacob's blessing on Judah, and gives four reasons why Saul hid himself.

debates: Why the lot was cast at all when Samuel had already anointed Saul privately.
Why Saul hid himself: modesty, unworthiness, certainty of the outcome, or the four considered grounds Henry supplies.
What "unto the Lord" implies was present at Mizpeh: the Urim, the ark, or the altar.
outliers: Ellicott observes that in one later tradition Saul's name is almost lost and he is known only as the tall one.

25.pericope_label: Then Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the Lord. And Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house. And Saul also went home to Gibeah; and there went with him a band of men, whose hearts God had touched. But the children of Belial said, How shall this man save us? And they despised him, and brought him no presents. But he held his peace.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the written "manner of the kingdom" for a charter limiting the king's power, supposes the same roll preserved the account of Saul's election and served the compiler of this book, and calls it the first trace of Israelite literary composition since Moses; Delitzsch explains the withheld present as the customary gift whose refusal amounted to rebellion.
Gill reports the contrary reading, that the document repeated the warning about arbitrary power as a testimony against the people, and identifies the malcontents as men of wealth from larger tribes.

Clarke supposes a compact between people and king, denies the band of men was military, and reads the withheld presents as tribute rather than ceremonial homage; Wesley makes the writing simply the laws by which the government was to be managed.
Henry holds both readings of the document at once, makes the band a remnant whose hearts God had touched, and reads Saul's forbearance as evidence that his title was sound.

debates: Whether the book Samuel wrote threatened the people with despotism or bound the king against it.
Who the band of men were: secret friends, proud fellow citizens, a mere escort, or a remnant divinely moved.
Whether the withheld presents were ceremonial homage or tribute owed to a public person.
outliers: Clarke compares the withheld presents to the free-will offerings by which Arab chiefs are still supplied in the villages where they encamp.
themes: Then Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the Lord. And Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house.
And Saul also went home to Gibeah; and there went with him a band of men, whose hearts God had touched.
But the children of Belial said, How shall this man save us? And they despised him, and brought him no presents. But he held his peace.
